newsitem.title: USA: Credit quality of US cardholders improves - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Credit quality of US cardholders improves - Moody's.

text.p: The credit quality of the average American credit card holder showed signs of improvement for the second consecutive month in June 1997, Moody's Investors Service reported.

U.S. credit card issuers wrote off 6.87 percent of account balances in credit card ABS pools in the month of June, a writeoff rate that exceeded the year-earlier level of 5.73 percent but represented a moderate improvement from the recent high of 7.10 percent in April 1997, according to Moody's monthly credit card indexes.
The sample pool used in the indexes currently includes some $223 billion of credit card receivables, Moody's said.

The delinquency rate, defined as the percent of credit card account balances in which a monthly payment is more than 30 days past due, declined for the fourth consecutive month in June 1997 to 5.23 percent, although it remained above the 4.68 percent seen in June 1996.

U.S. consumers repaid 13.24 percent of their credit card debt in June 1997, versus 11.97 percent a year earlier, for the highest year-to-year improvement in the principal payment rate index since December 1993, the rating agency reported.

For card holders, consumer debt has been growing at a slower pace while household incomes have steadied, trends that point to continuing improvement in credit quality. For card issuers, tighter underwriting and collection efforts begun early in 1996 appeared to be showing in the aggregate results.
"These trends continue to signal a potential stabilization in U.S. consumer credit quality by year end," said Moody's vice president Edward O. Bankole.

"We expect performance in securitized ABS pools to gradually stabilize as tighter underwriting standards, strengthened collections efforts, and rate repricing by card issuers start to improve the overall results," Bankole added.

However, Bankole also pointed out that "some caution is still warranted because of the broadened pool of credit cardholders over the last several years and the on-going increase in consumer bankruptcy filings."

Despite the improvements in June Bankole noted that "for the second quarter of 1997 as a whole, approximately 6.97 percent of bad credit card loans were written off, which was the highest level in the eight year history of Moody's chargeoff index, compared with the 5.52 percent rate in the second quarter of 1996.
However, the pace of deterioration was steady in the second quarter of 1997."
The delinquency rate averaged 5.31 percent at the end of the second quarter of 1997, up from 4.59 percent in the second quarter of 1996.

For investors in securities backed by credit card loans, the recent steep increases in the chargeoff rate have reduced the levels of excess spread -- the first layer of investor protection against losses in their securities -- to low levels. But the improving trend in revenues has mitigated some of that impact.

As a result, the three month average excess spread of 3.76 percent in June 1997 was down from 4.16 percent in June 1996, but remained healthy. Moody's defines excess spread as income earned in securitized credit card loan pools after deducting interest expenses on outstanding securities, servicing fees, and losses.

The current improvement in yield has partly cushioned the negative impact of rising losses on excess spread. Bankole said these factors indicated that most ABS investors remain adequately protected from credit losses in their investments.
